docs.title: Holdout Research
docs.text:
An independent systematic strategy research lab: each idea starts with an economic hypothesis, is tested on data it was never designed on (the holdout), and is written up honestly, including when it doesn't work.

What this is

A personal project by Nakul Pillai, built alongside an MSc in Financial Technology at Imperial College London. It is not a company or a live trading operation.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm Nakul Pillai, an MSc Financial Technology student at Imperial College London, with a BSc in Economics and Data Science from the University of Southampton.

Holdout Research is my personal research project: a place to develop trading strategy ideas with a consistent process and to document them honestly. The name comes from the holdout holdout, the data a strategy never sees while it is being designed, which is where every idea gets judged. It is not a company or a live trading operation.

  • GitHub: NakulPillai2407
  • LinkedIn: nakul-pillai

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: Every strategy here is tested to the same standard, and the standard gets stricter as the project goes on. This page describes the process as it is actually practised, including where earlier strategies fell short of it.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Hypothesis first. Each idea starts with an economic reason it might work and, just as importantly, a written list of results that would prove it wrong. This is done before any backtest is run.
  2. Freeze before testing. Every parameter is fixed in advance: lookback windows, thresholds, holding periods, cost assumptions and the decision rule. Anything changed afterwards is logged as a deviation, and results that depend on it are labelled exploratory.
  3. A holdout that is used once. The final stretch of data, usually the last 12 months, is kept out of the whole design process. It is evaluated a single time, after everything is frozen. If a result disappoints, the holdout is not reused to tune the strategy. A new hypothesis needs new data.
  4. Test the code before the data. Each backtest is first run on simulated data. A planted effect must be recovered, and a world with no effect must produce nothing. Only then is it run on real returns.
  5. Costs and benchmarks decide. The headline number is the Sharpe ratio after transaction costs, compared with simply holding the same stocks (equal-weight) and with a market index. Before-cost results are shown too, because they separate "no signal" from "a signal that costs eat".
  6. Report uncertainty. Key results come with confidence intervals (bootstrap) or standard errors that allow for autocorrelation (Newey-West), not bare point estimates.
  7. Publish the failures. Every idea and every variant goes in the Research Log, whether it worked or not.

docs.title: Standard testing process
docs.text: Step What is done Data Source, period and universe stated; look-ahead traced step by step; survivorship bias flagged where the universe is today's stocks Pre-registration Hypothesis, parameters and decision rule written down and frozen; "what would prove it wrong" stated Splits An in-sample period for design and a single-use holdout for evaluation Code validation Planted-effect and no-effect simulations before any real data Costs A proportional cost per trade, plus a sweep at higher costs Metrics Annualised return, volatility, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, turnover Benchmarks Equal-weight holding of the same stocks, plus a relevant market index Inference Bootstrap intervals and Newey-West t-statistics on the holdout Robustness Parameter sweeps and alternative specifications, labelled exploratory unless pre-registered Write-up Full report with limitations; deviations and failures stated

docs.title: Multiple testing
docs.text: The more variants that are tried, the more likely one looks good by chance. Every variant tried is recorded in the Research Log, and results are interpreted with that in mind. For example, two of 16 horizon estimates in HR-002 had p below 0.05, which is about what chance gives. Sweeps that were not pre-registered are labelled exploratory and are never used to claim a result. Adjustments such as the deflated Sharpe ratio will be added as the number of trials grows.

docs.title: HR-001: Lead-Lag Centrality
docs.text:
Status: Negative result (to revisit) Last updated: 2026-10-29 Asset class: US tech and semiconductor equities Code: lead-lag-centrality-strategy Report: Full report (PDF, 20 pages)

Headline result

Built exactly as specified and locked before the backtest ran, the strategy does not beat simply holding the same stocks, in sample or in the holdout. The reason is informative: neighbouring stocks do move with a hub, but almost entirely on the same day, so there is no multi-day catch-up to trade.

docs.title: 1. Hypothesis
docs.text:
Some stocks are watched much more closely than others. When one of these highly connected "hub" stocks makes a sharp move, economically linked but less-watched peers should not react straight away. They should catch up over the following days. The strategy is to watch hubs for a sharp move, then trade their connected peers in the same direction.

Why it might work. Analysts, passive index flows and algorithmic traders concentrate on the most liquid, most-covered names, so new information is priced into them almost immediately. Linked peers share real exposure through overlapping end demand, shared input costs or a common sector narrative, but get less continuous attention, so their prices should adjust more slowly. This is an instance of the gradual information diffusion and limited-attention literature (Hou and Moskowitz, 2005; Cohen and Frazzini, 2008), not a generic trend-following story.

Why this sector. US tech and semiconductors combine a few extremely heavily covered mega-caps with a long tail of smaller, less-watched but economically linked peers (equipment makers, smaller analog and EDA firms).

What would prove it wrong (stated in advance):

  • Connected peers move on the same day as the hub, with no measurable lag.
  • A real lag exists but does not produce a positive risk-adjusted return after realistic costs (5 to 10 bps round trip), especially in the holdout.
  • The apparent "lag" is fully explained by ordinary same-day correlation.

docs.title: 2. Data and universe
docs.text:
• Universe: 65 US tech and semiconductor tickers (mega-cap tech, semiconductor makers and equipment, smaller cloud and software names), plus the S&P 500 as a market benchmark.
  • Data: daily adjusted close prices from Yahoo Finance, from January 2019. Adjusted prices are used so splits and dividends do not appear as artificial jumps. The download is cached so every run uses an identical dataset.
  • Cleaning: JNPR returned no data and was dropped. Any stock missing more than 5% of its trading days was removed rather than patched. That removed 8 tickers: ABNB, ALGM, PLTR, SNOW, DDOG, NET and CRWD (listed after 2019), and QRVO (almost no usable data on Yahoo). The final universe is 56 stocks.
  • Gap filling: small gaps are filled only inside a stock's existing history and only up to 5 days. Nothing is extended before a first trading day or after a last one.
  • Known limitation: the universe is today's list of surviving names, not a point-in-time reconstruction (see Limitations).

docs.title: 3. Signal construction
docs.text:
All parameters were fixed before the backtest was run and never tuned afterwards.

  1. Weekly network. Each week, link two stocks if the correlation of their daily returns over the trailing 60 trading days exceeds 0.5. The network is rebuilt every week, giving 396 weekly networks.
  2. Hubs. Compute degree centrality (the share of the other stocks a stock is linked to). The six most connected stocks that week are the hubs.

  3. Shocks. A hub shock is flagged when a hub's daily return is more than twice its own trailing volatility, measured only up to the previous day:

    \[ |r_{h,t}| > 2\,\sigma_{h,t-1} \]

    This produced 736 shocks (639 in sample, 97 in the holdout). 4. Trade. At the next day's close, buy an equal-weighted basket of the hub's connected neighbours (short if the hub fell). Hold for 3 days. 5. Costs and sizing. 10 bps round-trip cost per trade. Capital is split equally across open trades, with no leverage. A position was open on about 48% of trading days.

Parameter Value Correlation window 60 trading days Correlation threshold 0.5 Hub measure Degree centrality, top 6 each week Shock trigger Return above 2x trailing volatility Holding period 3 days Transaction cost 10 bps round trip

Left: a typical week (7 Jan 2022), 439 links, one dense cluster with the hubs in red. Right: the stress week of 20 Jun 2025, 1,492 links, where almost every stock is tied to every other.

Which stocks became hubs. The most frequent hubs were MPWR, KLAC, ENTG, AMAT, LRCX, ADI, CDNS, MCHP, AVGO and SNPS: semiconductor equipment, analog and EDA names, not the mega-caps the hypothesis expected. Averaged over all weekly networks, AAPL ranks 29th of 56 on degree centrality, MSFT 18th, GOOGL 35th, AMZN 28th, META 45th, TSLA 53rd and NVDA 14th. Centrality here seems to reflect shared exposure to the semiconductor cycle rather than which stocks are most watched.

docs.title: 4. Backtest results
docs.text: The final 12 months were held out from the whole design process and used once, at the end. The in-sample period is about 6.5 years. Benchmarks are an equal-weighted holding of all 56 stocks and the S&P 500.

docs.title: In sample
docs.text: Series Cumulative return Annualised return Sharpe Max drawdown Sortino Win rate Strategy (with costs) -32.8% -5.9% -0.163 -57.1% -0.148 49.8% Strategy (no costs) -12.7% -2.1% 0.018 -49.9% 0.017 51.9% Equal-weight stocks 424.3% 28.8% 0.969 -40.8% 1.327 55.0% S&P 500 135.1% 14.0% 0.745 -33.9% 0.908 54.8%

docs.title: Holdout (final 12 months)
docs.text:
Series Cumulative return Annualised return Sharpe Max drawdown Sortino Win rate Strategy (with costs) 9.5% 9.5% 0.453 -18.2% 0.458 50.0% Strategy (no costs) 14.1% 14.1% 0.590 -17.7% 0.595 50.4% Equal-weight stocks 48.7% 48.9% 1.582 -14.6% 2.480 57.0% S&P 500 15.7% 15.7% 1.211 -9.1% 1.857 53.0%

Reading the results.

  • Both benchmarks beat the strategy on every metric in both periods: higher Sharpe and Sortino, smaller drawdowns.
  • The win rate is about 50% in both periods, essentially a coin flip on the bets it makes.
  • Removing costs lifts the in-sample Sharpe from -0.163 to about flat (0.018), so part of the in-sample loss comes from trading too often relative to the size of the edge, not only from a weak signal.
  • The holdout Sharpe (0.453) is better than the in-sample one, which is unusual and a reason for caution rather than celebration, given how sensitive it is to the threshold (below).
  • Cumulative returns across the two periods are not directly comparable because of their different lengths. Annualised return, Sharpe and Sortino are the right comparison.

docs.title: Does the mechanism exist? The lag test
docs.text:
The test that mattered most checks the mechanism directly: how do a hub's neighbours move on the shock day and the days after?

Day after hub shock Average neighbour move (bps, in the hub's direction) Day 0 (shock day) +380 Day 1 -46 Day 2 about +27 Day 3 about +8

Neighbours move strongly with the hub, but the move is absorbed almost entirely on the shock day. A real catch-up would show later days growing toward the day-0 size. Instead, day 1 is slightly negative. There is essentially no multi-day catch-up to trade, so the weak performance is a property of the hypothesis, not a bug in the pipeline.

docs.title: Correlation threshold sensitivity
docs.text:
Only the threshold was stress-tested. The 0.5 value was fixed in advance and kept.

Threshold Holdout Sharpe 0.4 -0.318 0.5 (locked) 0.453 0.6 0.249

The result is not stable: it is negative at 0.4 and positive at 0.5 and 0.6. The single positive result at 0.5 should be treated with caution.

docs.title: Network behaviour in stress
docs.text: The median network density at 0.5 is 28%. In market-wide stress it saturates: in the week of 20 June 2025 (whose window covers the April 2025 tariff sell-off), 97% of all pairs were linked. When almost everything is connected, degree centrality stops separating hubs from the rest, and the hub and neighbour distinction the strategy relies on effectively disappears.

docs.title: Pitfall checks
docs.text:
• Look-ahead bias: traced end to end on the first shock in the sample (network built on 29 Mar 2019, volatility measured to 2 Apr, shock on 3 Apr, trade entered on 4 Apr). Every step only uses information available before it, confirmed by an explicit check in the code.
  • Data snooping: all parameters were committed to before the result was known.
  • Holdout validation: the last 12 months were used once, at the end.

docs.title: 6. What went wrong and limitations
docs.text:
• The mechanism is not there at daily frequency. Connected stocks move together on the same day, which the network captures, but there is no lagged catch-up.
  • Survivorship bias. The universe is today's 56 surviving stocks (JNPR, for example, disappeared after HPE acquired it in 2025). This most likely inflates absolute returns for both the strategy and its equal-weight benchmark, so the underperformance finding holds up better than the raw returns do. A point-in-time constituents list would fix this.
  • Costs and slippage are simplified. The 10 bps cost is applied once per trade and does not scale with position size or the liquidity of the neighbour stocks.
  • Concentration risk. The hubs cluster in semiconductor equipment and analog names. A shock to that slice of the supply chain could trigger several trades at once that are really the same bet, so splitting capital equally would not diversify anything.
  • Capacity. The number of shocks per year is fixed by the signal, so more capital would either concentrate in the same neighbour stocks or sit idle.
  • No risk reduction. The strategy's drawdown was worse than both benchmarks in both periods.
  • Sensitivity. Only the threshold was stress-tested, and it was not robust. The window length, hold period, shock size and number of hubs were never tested the same way.

docs.title: 7. Next steps
docs.text:
• Test the lag first. If repeated, check the mechanism directly before building a full backtest around it.
  • Intraday lag. Any delayed reaction may exist within the day, at minute or hourly level, which daily data cannot see. This is an open question, not a ruled-out one.
  • Point-in-time universe to remove survivorship bias.
  • Broader parameter sensitivity across the window, hold period, shock size and number of hubs.
  • Realistic slippage model that depends on position size and liquidity.
  • Alternative centrality measures (eigenvector, betweenness) and non-semiconductor universes.

docs.title: HR-002: News Sentiment
docs.text:
Status: Negative result Last updated: 2026-10-29 Asset class: US large-cap equities Code: news-sentiment-research Reports: Daily test (PDF) and intraday test (PDF)

Headline result

Tested twice, once with daily news and once with exact release times and 1-minute prices, trading on the sentiment of a headline does not beat simply holding the same stocks. Sentiment is strongly linked to returns on the day of the article, but by the time a trade can be placed, what is left is a few basis points, below the cost of trading it.

docs.title: 1. Hypothesis
docs.text:
When a company gets clearly good or bad news, the market does not finish pricing it in at once. A stock's abnormal return should keep moving in the direction of the news after the headline is out, by more than it costs to trade. The strategy is to score each headline with FinBERT, buy after clearly positive news and short after clearly negative news.

Why it might work. The tone of a story is soft, qualitative information that is harder to price than a number such as an earnings surprise. Prices have been found to under-react to negative words in firm news (Tetlock, Saar-Tsechansky and Macskassy, 2008) and to drift after bad headlines (Chan, 2003), and attention is limited and uneven (Barber and Odean, 2008). The evidence is not one-sided: media pessimism can also reverse rather than drift (Tetlock, 2007). In liquid US large caps, where algorithms read the same feeds within seconds, the reaction may well be over before a trade can be placed.

What would prove it wrong (stated in advance):

  • The in-sample coefficient of the abnormal return on the sentiment score, at the trading horizon, is not positive and significant at 5%.
  • The holdout net-of-cost Sharpe ratio does not beat the equal-weight benchmark.

Both had to hold. Neither did, in either test.

docs.title: 2. Data and universe
docs.text:
Test 1: daily Test 2: intraday News FNSPID, dated to the day Alpaca (Benzinga), exact release time Prices Daily adjusted closes 1-minute bars (IEX feed) Period 2021 to 2023 January 2024 to September 2026 Holdout Last 12 months, used once Last 12 months, used once Universe 50 US stocks drawn at random across industries 50 US stocks drawn at random from the 84 most heavily covered Time of day Date only, no release time Exact release time Unit of observation Stock-day: the mean score of that day's articles (15,592 stock-days from 28,078 articles) One article-ticker pair (25,049, regular-hours releases only) Text scored Headline, plus the summary where the file has one Headline only

Multi-stock roundup articles are removed, because they say nothing about one stock, but the rule differs: the daily test drops a headline that appears on three or more of the universe's stocks on the same day, the intraday test drops articles tagged with more than two tickers. In the intraday test only articles released in regular hours are traded, since an after-hours article could only be traded at the next open. Both universes were drawn using article counts and a fixed seed, never prices.

docs.title: 3. Signal construction
docs.text:
All parameters were written down before the data was seen, and later changes are logged as dated deviations in each study's PARAMETERS.md.

  1. Score. The headline's FinBERT score is the probability of positive minus the probability of negative, from -1 to +1. VADER is the comparison model.
  2. Signal. Long at +0.5 or above, short at -0.5 or below.
  3. Abnormal return. The stock's return minus its beta times the market's return, with beta estimated only from days before the event.
  4. Entry and exit. Test 1 enters at the close of the article's date and holds one day. Test 2 enters at the open of the first minute bar starting at least 60 seconds after the release and holds 60 minutes, or to the close if that comes first.
  5. Costs and sizing. 10 bps round trip (20 and 30 bps as checks), equal weight across the day's trades, no leverage, one open position per stock.

docs.title: 4. Backtest results
docs.text:
Measure Test 1 in sample Test 1 held out Test 2 in sample Test 2 held out Cumulative return, after costs -42.0% -9.8% -39.8% -17.8% Cumulative return, before costs -6.2% +13.1% -6.8% +5.7% Sharpe ratio, after costs -0.81 -0.34 -5.04 -3.74 Sharpe ratio, before costs 0.04 0.66 -0.68 1.09 Equal-weight stocks, Sharpe 0.39 0.94 1.69 1.18 Max drawdown, after costs -48.1% -20.1% -39.7% -17.8%

Net returns in Test 2 look extreme because a 10 bps cost is charged on capital every day a trade is open, which compounds. The before-cost rows are the fairer read of whether there is a signal. Even before costs, neither test beat the equal-weight benchmark in the holdout (0.66 against 0.94, and 1.09 against 1.18).

docs.title: Where the effect is
docs.text:
Abnormal return per unit of sentiment In sample Holdout Test 1, article's own day +110.2 bps (t = 4.65) +78.1 bps (t = 4.40) Test 1, next day (the trade) +9.7 bps (p = 0.30) +8.1 bps (p = 0.34) Test 2, 60 minutes after entry (the trade) +3.95 bps (p = 0.56) +4.0 bps (p = 0.10)

Sentiment is tightly tied to the move on the day of the article, which a trader cannot capture. What is left after the release is about the size of the cost or smaller.

Test 1: average abnormal return in the direction of the sentiment, after days with strong sentiment (1,981 in sample, 861 in the holdout; the chart's "out-of-sample" label means the holdout). The move is concentrated on day 0. The green bar, day 1, is the one the strategy trades, and it is small.

docs.title: 5. Robustness
docs.text:
The checks below are for the intraday test unless a line says otherwise. The daily test also ran thresholds of 0.3 and 0.7, VADER in place of FinBERT and a no-cost version, all in its report; its net Sharpe at a 0.3 threshold is -0.95 in sample and -0.17 held out.

  • Horizons. Test 2 also looked at 5, 15, 30, 120, 180, 240 and 300 minutes. All 16 estimates (8 horizons, 2 periods) are positive, from about 1 to 8 bps, and none beats the cost. Two have p below 0.05 (5 and 120 minutes, holdout), which is about what chance gives across 16 tests.

Net Sharpe at a 10 bps cost for each holding period, in sample and in the holdout. Only 60 minutes (dotted line) was pre-specified; the rest are exploratory. Every horizon is negative, and longer holds lose less only because they trade less often.

  • Thresholds and model. Net Sharpe is negative at every threshold (0.3, 0.5 and 0.7) and for both FinBERT and VADER, in both periods.
  • Costs. At 20 and 30 bps the 60-minute holdout Sharpe falls from -3.74 to -8.57 and -13.40.
  • Standard errors. Clustering by date instead of by stock gives the same answer.
  • Code checks. Both notebooks were run on simulated data first: a planted effect was recovered, and a world with no effect gave nothing.

docs.title: 6. What went wrong and limitations
docs.text:
• The reaction is over before a trade can act. Daily data cannot show this, and minute data shows it directly.
  • The first design was replaced. Test 1 began as a delayed three-day hold. That was swapped for an entry at the close of the article's date after the first results were seen, because the hypothesis was always to trade straight after the news. It is logged as a post-hoc deviation, so Test 1's holdout result is exploratory.
  • The daily test has a known bias in its favour. Its news file has dates but no times, so some articles dated D were published after the close of D, and entering at that close is then slightly ahead of the information. This flatters the daily strategy, and it still lost.
  • Heavily covered stocks only. The universes are today's well-known US stocks, where the market is fastest. Survivorship bias is likely.
  • Free price feed. Test 2 uses the IEX feed, which carries part of market volume, so prices are approximate and some minutes have no bar. About 3.5% of signals were skipped for stale bars.
  • Costs are simplified. A flat 10 bps ignores the wider spread just after a release and the cost of borrowing stock to short.
  • Exploratory leads are not results. A 0.7 threshold had the best holdout Sharpe before costs (2.16), but in sample the same setting was negative (-0.83) and its holdout Sharpe after costs was still -2.09. Treat it as noise until it replicates on new data.

docs.title: 7. Next steps
docs.text:
• Tick-level data and faster execution, to test the first seconds after release.
  • Measure the return in the minutes before each article, to see how much of the move had already happened.
  • A spread and size cost model, with borrowing costs on shorts.
  • Smaller and less covered stocks, where the market may be slower.
  • A later period or new stocks to test the holdout leads.
  • Scoring full article text and separating first reports from repeats.

docs.title: HR-003: Sector Residual Reversion
docs.text:
Status: Negative result Last updated: 2026-10-29 Asset class: US large-cap equities (S&P 500 members, point in time) Code: sector-residual-reversion Report: Full report (PDF, 20 pages)

Headline result

On a holdout that was run once, after every rule was frozen, the strategy lost money before costs and far more after them. The pre-registered rule returns NOT SUPPORTED: the reversal coefficient is -0.0040 (t = -0.66), the gross Sharpe ratio is -0.24 with an interval that includes zero, and the net Sharpe ratio at 5 bp per side is -4.02. The book trades about 1.77 times its size every day, so costs alone take roughly 22% a year.

docs.title: 1. Hypothesis
docs.text:
When a large US stock moves sharply for reasons specific to that company, rather than because its whole sector moved, part of that move should reverse the next day. The strategy removes the part of each stock's return that its sector ETF explains, scales what is left (the residual) by its recent volatility, buys the unusually negative ones and shorts the unusually positive ones. An ETF position cancels the leftover sector exposure, so the book is dollar-neutral and close to market-neutral.

Why it might work. A move that follows from sector news is more likely to be information and so should stick. The stock-specific leftover is more likely to come from one-sided trading that pushes the price away from fair value for a day, and that part should revert. Short-term reversal is an old, well-documented effect (Jegadeesh, 1990; Lehmann, 1990), residual and ETF-hedged versions are discussed by Avellaneda and Lee (2010), and a standing concern is that the gross profits have shrunk and that costs absorb what is left (Nagel, 2012). This study does not claim a new idea. It tests an old one properly.

What would prove it wrong (stated in advance):

  • H1a. The holdout Fama-MacBeth coefficient of the next-day residual on today's residual is not negative with a Newey-West t-statistic below -2.
  • H1b. The holdout net Sharpe ratio at 5 bp per side does not have a 95% bootstrap interval entirely above zero, or the alpha against SPY does not have t above 2.

SUPPORTED needs both. GROSS-ONLY means H1a holds, the gross Sharpe interval is above zero and H1b fails. Anything else is NOT SUPPORTED. My prior, written down before any data was downloaded, was GROSS-ONLY: a detectable effect before costs that does not survive costs.

docs.title: 2. Data and universe
docs.text:
• Universe: S&P 500 members at each date, across all 11 GICS sectors, each hedged against its SPDR sector ETF. A stock needs a prior close of at least $5. Benchmark: SPY.
  • Membership: rebuilt from today's Wikipedia constituent list (503 tickers) by undoing the index additions and removals, working backwards. Five reconstruction issues are logged, not silently fixed.
  • Prices: Yahoo Finance daily data. The download is cached and hashed. There are no delisting returns.
  • Windows: in sample 2018-10-01 to 2023-12-31 (1,321 sessions); holdout 2024-01-01 to 2026-09-30 (689 sessions), used once. The raw prices were split into the two files at download.
  • Coverage: the share of point-in-time members that could be traded rose from 86.0% in 2018 to 99.0% in 2026, because removed stocks often have no free prices.
  • Known limitation: survivorship bias is reduced, not removed (see Limitations).

docs.title: 3. Signal construction
docs.text:
All parameters were fixed before the build and never tuned.

  1. Residual. For each stock and day, beta is a 60-day rolling OLS slope on its sector ETF using data through the previous day (at least 50 observations). The residual is

    \[ e_{i,t} = r_{i,t} - \beta_{i,t-1}\, r_{\text{ETF},t} \]

  2. Signal. \( z_{i,t} = e_{i,t} / \sigma_{i,t-1} \), where \( \sigma_{i,t-1} \) is the trailing 60-day standard deviation of residuals through the previous day.

  3. Trade. Long stocks with z of -1 or lower, short stocks with z of +1 or higher. Each leg carries 0.5 gross. The ETF hedge cancels the net sector beta of the stock positions. The signal is read at the close of day t, entered at the open of t+1 and exited at the open of t+2.
  4. Costs. 5 bp per side on stocks (2 and 10 bp as sensitivities), 1 bp per side on the ETF hedge and a flat 50 bp a year borrow on shorts.
Parameter Value Beta window 60 trading days (minimum 50) z-score window 60 trading days (minimum 50) Threshold z of -1 or lower (long), +1 or higher (short) Holding period 1 day, rebuilt daily Minimum price $5 Stock cost 5 bp per side Inference Fama-MacBeth with Newey-West (5 lags); stationary bootstrap, 10,000 resamples

Holdout z over eligible stock-days, clipped at +/-8 (log scale). 24.3% of eligible stock-days have an absolute z of 1 or more.

The code was tested before it saw any real return: it recovers a planted reversal (coefficient -0.0984 against a planted -0.10), finds nothing in a null world (3.0% of simulations with |t| above 2) and finds nothing when each stock is hedged against a deliberately wrong ETF. 13 unit tests, including look-ahead tests, pass.

docs.title: 4. Backtest results
docs.text: The holdout was used once, after the freeze. Gross and net results are shown for the primary specification.

docs.title: Holdout (2024-01-01 to 2026-09-30)
docs.text:
Series Annual return Sharpe (95% CI) Max drawdown Gross -1.5% -0.24 (-1.47, 0.96) -14.4% Net, 2 bp per side -12.1% -1.91 (-3.14, -0.69) -32.8% Net, 5 bp per side -25.5% -4.02 (-5.39, -2.75) -52.2% Net, 10 bp per side -47.8% -7.53 (-9.22, -6.10) -73.0% SPY buy-and-hold n/a 0.98 (0.00, 2.18) n/a Equal-weight 11 sector ETFs n/a 0.79 (-0.14, 1.99) n/a

Reading the results.

  • The holdout coefficient is -0.0040 (Newey-West t = -0.66), about one twenty-fifth of the planted effect the code recovers in simulation. The sign is as hypothesised but it cannot be told from zero.
  • Alpha against SPY is -26.0% a year (t = -6.50) with a beta of 0.029. It is negative because costs drag on a market-neutral book, not because of a bet against the market.
  • The breakeven cost per side was 0.18 bp in sample and -0.71 bp in the holdout. A negative breakeven means the strategy lost money even with free trading.
  • The holdout can only detect a Sharpe ratio of about 1.19 or more, so a modest real gross edge could have been missed. The honest reading is no detectable effect and a clear cost failure, not proof that no reversal exists.
Decision rule (holdout) Value Met? H1a: coefficient negative, Newey-West t below -2 -0.0040, t = -0.66 No H1b(i): net Sharpe at 5 bp, interval above 0 -4.02, (-5.38, -2.75) No H1b(ii): alpha vs SPY with t above 2 -26.0% a year, t = -6.50 No GROSS-ONLY: H1a plus gross Sharpe interval above 0 H1a fails; (-1.46, 1.01) No

Note: the decision-rule intervals differ slightly from the results table above (for example -5.38 vs -5.39). The source report discloses the small difference; it was not investigated and does not change any conclusion.

Verdict: NOT SUPPORTED. This is weaker than my prior, because the gross effect was not detectable either.

docs.title: Sectors
docs.text: Only Utilities shows a holdout gross Sharpe interval entirely above zero (1.46, interval 0.12 to 2.77; net at 5 bp 0.11). With 11 sectors and several tests that is what chance alone produces. In sample, Materials and Industrials stood out and neither held up in the holdout. I draw no conclusion from any of these.

docs.title: Pitfall checks
docs.text:
• Look-ahead bias: beta and the z denominator at day t use data through day t-1, checked by unit tests. A further test confirms that profit and loss does not depend on future data.
  • Overfitting and snooping: parameters, windows and the decision rule were fixed before any data was seen. The holdout was run once. Exploratory variants are labelled.
  • Holdout discipline: the code refuses to load holdout prices unless a lock file exists and refuses to run the holdout twice.

docs.title: 6. What went wrong and limitations
docs.text:
• Costs decide the result. Turnover is about 1.77 times the book per day (about 446 a year). There is no gross edge to pay for it.
  • Survivorship bias. Reduced, not removed. In sample, only 48% of the 157 removed members have usable data, against 100% of the survivors, and there are no delisting returns.
  • Current sector labels are applied to the whole sample. Visa, Mastercard and PayPal were Information Technology until March 2023, which is why they are excluded in a robustness check.
  • Idealised execution. Fills are assumed at the open, borrow is a flat 50 bp a year, and there is no market impact or capacity estimate.
  • Low power. About 2.75 years of holdout can only detect a Sharpe of 1.19 or more.
  • Beta timing mismatch. Betas are estimated on close-to-close returns but applied to open-to-open holds.
  • Free data. Yahoo prices can contain errors. 11 in-sample and 20 holdout daily moves above 50% were kept as downloaded. At least one former member's ticker (STI) has prices that appear to belong to another company, but its membership and price dates never overlap, so it could not be traded.
  • Dates. The pre-registration dates are my own record. The published repo has no local git history, so it cannot prove when anything was written.
  • Deviations. Four were logged, none changing a pre-registered parameter or the decision rule (see the repo's DEVIATIONS.md).

docs.title: 7. Next steps
docs.text:
• Realistic execution: an intraday check of the open fills with a spread and impact model, and borrow costs by stock.
  • Better data: a re-run on a survivorship-free source such as Bloomberg or WRDS, with delisting returns and historical sector labels. The data layer is built so this does not touch the signal code. It has not been done.
  • Lower turnover: a separate, pre-registered study of longer holds or a stronger threshold, as a new hypothesis on a new holdout and not a rescue of this one.
  • Combination: test whether a residual-reversion signal adds anything beside the news-sentiment work, on the shared holdout calendar.
